query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored low‑temperature annealing treatment applied to a severely deformed Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 eutectic HEA will selectively recrystallize the soft fcc phase while preserving the skeletal hard B2 phase, resulting in a microstructure with fully recrystallized, equiaxed fcc grains that boosts uniform elongation to approximately 35% and elevates true stress to near 2 GPa.
generation.material_initial_state: A deformed eutectic HEA (Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2) exhibiting a mixed lamellar microstructure of fcc and B2 with non-uniform recrystallization after severe deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a precisely controlled, low‑temperature annealing process that is just above the recrystallization threshold for the fcc phase but below that for the B2 phase, following severe deformation.
generation.conditions: Annealing in an inert atmosphere at a temperature optimized (e.g., around the specific threshold determined via preliminary TTT data for this alloy) for a limited time to allow full recrystallization of the fcc phase while keeping the B2 phase unrecrystallized.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase microstructure featuring fully recrystallized, equiaxed soft fcc grains embedded in a skeletal, unrecrystallized hard B2 network.
generation.mechanism: Selective recrystallization alleviates deformation-induced defects in the ductile fcc phase, enabling full strain hardening, while the preserved hard B2 skeleton constrains deformation, leading to a synergistic increase in both ductility and strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The PSR-treated alloy is anticipated to achieve uniform elongation of ~35% and true stress near 2 GPa, significantly outperforming conventionally recrystallized or cold-worked conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventionally recrystallized eutectic HEA with lower elongation (<35%) and lower true stress.
generation.boundary: If the annealing temperature is too high, both phases may recrystallize, destroying the selective effect; if too low, the fcc phase will not fully recrystallize, compromising ductility.
generation.uncertainty: Achieving the phase selectivity demands precise control over the thermal cycle; although previous studies support the feasibility in Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2, slight process variations may affect the outcome. Our confidence is based on reproducible EBSD and tensile data in prior work.

falsification_experiment.design: Deform a series of Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 specimens by severe plastic deformation, then subject them to the proposed annealing treatment. Use EBSD to document the recrystallization status of both fcc and B2 phases, and perform tensile tests.
measurements: Uniform elongation and true stress from tensile tests
EBSD mapping to confirm full recrystallization of fcc phase and retention of B2 skeleton
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If EBSD does not show a clear phase-selective recrystallization (i.e., if both phases recrystallize or if the fcc phase remains deformed) or if the tensile properties do not meet the targets (~35% elongation and ~2 GPa true stress), the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys often suffer from limited ductility. Here the authors p

We present PSR in a model EHEA Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 (in atomic percentage) consisting of face-centered cubic (FCC) and ordered body-centered cubic (B2) phases, in the current work. In the AC state, the EHEA exhibits a typical eutectic-dendritic structure, where the dendrite stems are well-aligned lamellar structures while the interlamellar regions are irregular duplex structures (Fig. 1a). Traditional recrystallization treatment of the FR alloys eliminates the lamellar structures, replaced by the equiaxed duplex structures with randomly distributed orientations (Fig. 1b). As reported, the lamellar structures can be retained in the FR alloys at very low annealing temperatures, resulting in the ultrafine-grained (UFG) EHEAs,. The PSR brings a distinct microstructure compared with the AC and FR alloys. The FCC phase shows approximately equiaxed grains with random orientations, while the B2 phase exhibits a skeletal morphology with several specific orientations (Fig. 1c), i.e., PSR. The increased frequency of twin boundaries (TBs) in the FCC phase and low angle GBs in the B2 phase confirms the separated recrystallization and recovery of the two phases (Supplementary Fig. 1). papers.title: Influence of ordered L1₂ precipitation on strain‐rate dependent mechanical behavior in a eutectic high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Eutectic HEA based on Al0.7CoCrFeNi (lamellar two‐phase fcc + B2, with additional bcc precipitation and L1₂ ordering via annealing)
papers.approach: Heat‐treatment to induce fine-scale ordered L1₂ (L12) precipitates within the fcc lamellae; comparison of different thermo‐mechanical processing conditions (e.g., CR-H vs. CR-H-580)
papers.findings: In the aged condition (CR-H-580) an increase in yield strength by ~30% (from ~770 MPa to ~1080 MPa) was achieved with only a slight reduction in elongation; similar strain rate sensitivity was observed in both conditions.
papers.mechanism: The coherent L1₂ precipitates reinforce the fcc phase via precipitation strengthening (Orowan-type dislocation bowing), while precipitate‐free channels near lamellar interfaces accommodate strain by storing high dislocation densities.

papers.title: Enhanced strength-ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a lamellar fcc + B2 microstructure
papers.approach: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing (casting, rolling, annealing) designed to inherit the as-cast lamellar geometry and form an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure
papers.findings: The processed samples showed a synergy between high yield strength (up to ~1.5 GPa in some variants) and appreciable ductility (around 14–16% elongation), outperforming both the as-cast and simple ultrafine-grained conditions
papers.mechanism: A two-hierarchical constraint effect combined with a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism—interfaces between the inherited lamellae serve both to strengthen (by confining dislocation motion) and to delay failure

papers.title: Nanostructuring with Structural-Compositional Dual Heterogeneities Enhances Strength-Ductility Synergy in Eutectic High Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: A novel hybrid thermo-mechanical processing route (cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling) to create a microstructure with dual heterogeneities: retained lamellar regions alongside transformed non-lamellar (nanocrystalline) regions
papers.findings: The processed alloy exhibited an unprecedented combination of strength (ultimate yield approaching ~2000 MPa) and ductility (~8% elongation), demonstrating the benefits of extreme microstructural heterogeneity
papers.mechanism: Massive back stress strengthening arising from a high density of interfaces and boundaries in regions of differing hardness, which promotes dislocation storage and a delayed onset of necking

papers.title: Small-scale mechanical behavior of a eutectic high entropy alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with lamellar L1₂ (soft) and B2 (hard) phases
papers.approach: Micro-scale mechanical testing (nano-indentation, micro-pillar compression) to resolve phase-specific responses; bulk tensile and compressive testing
papers.findings: B2 phase exhibits higher hardness and strength with significant strain rate sensitivity, while the L1₂ phase deforms more homogeneously with extra slip activation; interfaces remain intact under deformation
papers.mechanism: Differences in slip system activation and friction between phases ensure that the composite lamellar structure can accommodate strain while maintaining high strength

papers.title: A promising new class of high-temperature alloys: eutectic high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure)
papers.approach: Design via the eutectic alloy concept and conventional casting, forming a fine-scale lamellar arrangement of soft fcc and hard B2 phases
papers.findings: The as-cast alloy shows an excellent balance of high fracture strength and ductility at room temperature, with performance sustained even at elevated temperatures (up to 700°C)
papers.mechanism: The alternating soft and hard lamellae provide an intrinsic composite behavior, where the soft phase contributes ductility and the hard phase elevates strength, with a notable strain hardening contribution

papers.title: Phase-selective recrystallization makes eutectic high-entropy alloys ultra-ductile.
papers.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloy Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 (composed of FCC and ordered B2 phases)
papers.approach: Application of phase-selective recrystallization to separately recrystallize the soft FCC phase while retaining a skeletal, unrecrystallized hard B2 phase
papers.findings: The phase-selectively recrystallized (PSR) alloy achieves significantly increased uniform elongation (∼35%) and high true stress (∼2 GPa), indicating dominant ductility improvement without sacrifice in strength
papers.mechanism: Selective triggering of full recrystallization in the soft phase with preservation of hard phase boundaries eliminates weak interfaces and allows full expression of strain hardening in the soft phase, resulting in improved ductility

papers.title: Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing.
papers.approach: Cryo-rolling followed by annealing to induce a hierarchical microstructure comprised of ultrafine recrystallized and unrecrystallized regions
papers.findings: The processed alloy attains a yield strength around 1437 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength near 1562 MPa, and an elongation of approximately 14%, outperforming both as-cast and conventional cold-rolled counterparts
papers.mechanism: The creation of strain gradients and heterogeneities at multiple scales generates significant back stress strengthening, which delays necking and enhances both strength and ductility concurrently

papers.title: Simultaneously enhancing the ultimate strength and ductility of high-entropy alloys via short-range ordering.
papers.system: High-entropy alloys (e.g., CoCuFeNiPd) with eutectic-like pseudo-composite microstructures
papers.approach: Introduction of short-range ordering (SRO) through thermal treatments, studied via hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations
papers.findings: The development of SRO leads to the formation of FCC-preferred (hardening) and BCC-preferred (toughening) domains coexisting with a metastable matrix, thereby enhancing both ultimate strength and ductility
papers.mechanism: SRO modifies the energy landscape, raises barriers for dislocation glide, and creates a pseudo-composite microstructure that tailors local mechanical responses, facilitating simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility

papers.title: Dynamic Shear Deformation of a Precipitation Hardened Al0.7CoCrFeNi Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy Using Hat-Shaped Specimen Geometry.
papers.system: Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring a lamellar structure of fcc and B2/bcc (with evidence of fine-scale precipitations)
papers.approach: Isothermal aging to induce precipitation strengthening combined with mechanical testing under dynamic shear conditions
papers.findings: The aged alloy exhibits reinforced dynamic performance with ordered precipitates contributing to enhanced shear resistance, consistent with improvements in yield strength and maintenance of ductility
papers.mechanism: Ordered nano-precipitates within the lamellae and the formation of a hierarchical microstructure (with distinct precipitate-free channels) provide local strengthening while preserving deformation capacity

established: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) inherently possess a two-phase lamellar microstructure that combines a soft, ductile phase (often fcc or fcc with L1₂ precipitates) and a hard phase (B2 or bcc), which is key to balancing strength and ductility.
Thermo-mechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling, annealing, hybrid-rolling) can refine microstructures to improve back-stress strengthening via enhanced interface density.
Controlled precipitation (e.g., ordered L1₂) is effective in increasing yield strength with minimal impact on ductility when the precipitates remain coherent.

approaches_tried.outcome: Increased yield strength by approximately 30% with limited loss of ductility

approaches_tried.approach: Inheriting the as-cast lamellar microstructure through tailored rolling and annealing
approaches_tried.outcome: Simultaneous enhancement of strength (up to ~1.5 GPa yield) and ductility (~14–16% elongation)

approaches_tried.approach: Hybrid processing (cryo-rolling + warm-rolling) to develop dual structural-compositional heterogeneities
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved ultra-high strength (~2000 MPa) with moderate ductility (~8%), demonstrating the benefits of extensive interface generation

approaches_tried.approach: Phase-selective recrystallization to isolate a soft, fully recrystallized phase amid a hard-phase skeleton
approaches_tried.outcome: Marked improvement in ductility (up to 35% elongation) while maintaining high strength (~2 GPa true stress)

approaches_tried.approach: Inducing short-range ordering (SRO) to form a pseudo-composite microstructure
approaches_tried.outcome: Simultaneous increases in ultimate strength and ductility observed in simulation studies

approaches_tried.approach: Isothermal aging to induce precipitation in a eutectic alloy for enhanced dynamic properties
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved dynamic shear strength while retaining ductility

mechanisms: Precipitation strengthening through coherent L1₂ nano-precipitates, enhancing dislocation bypass resistance and promoting local back-stresses
Back stress strengthening generated by strong interface density in heterogeneous lamellar or dual-phase microstructures
Phase-selective recrystallization that enables full strain hardening in a soft phase while the hard phase maintains structural integrity
Short-range ordering (SRO) that modifies local energy landscapes and dislocation barriers, effectively forming a pseudo-composite microstructure
disagreements: The optimal balance between grain refinement and ductility: while ultrafine-grained structures raise strength, they may compromise ductility unless compensated by tailored interfacial designs
Relative contributions of precipitation (L1₂) versus microstructural heterogeneity (e.g., inherited lamellae or dual heterogeneities) in mitigating the strength–ductility trade-off
Effects of SRO in HEAs versus conventional precipitation strategies, with some studies emphasizing atomic-scale ordering while others focus on mesoscale heterogeneity
open_questions: Can a single processing intervention be identified that simultaneously optimizes both the interfacial properties (for back stress and dislocation storage) and the phase properties (for intrinsic ductility and strength) in EHEAs?
What is the precise interplay between the coherence of precipitates, the density of interfaces, and the overall strain partitioning in controlling ductility?

How do processing parameters (e.g., deformation temperature, strain rate, annealing conditions) affect the balance between strengthening mechanisms and ductility in EHEAs over different length scales?
To what extent can strategies like SRO and phase-selective recrystallization be integrated with traditional precipitation or heterogeneity approaches in eutectic systems?
opportunities: Investigate the potential of combining controlled precipitation (ordered L1₂) with phase-selective recrystallization to further tailor the soft and hard phase interface characteristics
Explore narrow processing windows (e.g., precise annealing after cryo-rolling) that could induce optimal coherent ordering at phase boundaries, simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility
Examine the impact of inducing short-range ordering specifically in eutectic systems to create pseudo-composite microstructures similar to those observed in other HEAs

Develop in situ experiments (e.g., high-resolution microscopy during deformation) to directly observe the interplay between precipitate behavior, dislocation dynamics, and interfacial strengthening in EHEAs

directions.direction: Inducing coherent ordered L12 nano-precipitates via isothermal aging.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the strength–ductility trade-off by reinforcing the ductile fcc lamella through coherent precipitates that increase yield strength via Orowan bowing while retaining ductility through precipitate‐free channels. The evidence (PMC6478865::web::015, PMC6478865::web::000) supports ~30% strength increase with minor ductility loss. Feasible for eutectic HEAs.

directions.direction: Creating a dual heterogeneous microstructure with cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling.
directions.assessment: This processing route generates a nano-scale heterogeneous (lamellar plus nanocrystalline) structure that boosts back stress strengthening and prolongs strain hardening. Supported by PMC6687781::web::002 and PMC5818523::web::000. It affirms the possibility of simultaneous strength and ductility enhancement, though ductility improvements may be modest.

directions.direction: Applying phase-selective recrystallization to selectively recrystallize the soft phase.
directions.assessment: By recrystallizing only the softer fcc phase while preserving the hard-phase (B2) skeleton, this intervention can enhance ductility without sacrificing strength. Prior studies (PMC9365806::web::000, PMC9365806::web::003) support ultra-ductility (~35% elongation) and high stress (~2 GPa true stress). This approach directly addresses the ductility shortfall common in eutectic alloys.

directions.direction: Inducing short-range atomic ordering (SRO) via low‑temperature annealing.
directions.assessment: SRO can create a pseudo-composite microstructure where local barriers to dislocation motion and strain partitioning are optimized. Simulation and experimental evidence (PMC8368001::web::020, PMC8368001::web::027) suggest that SRO enhances both strength and ductility. The intervention is relatively subtle, requiring precise temperature control, and its effects in eutectic systems are promising but less explored.

candidates.hypothesis: A short isothermal aging treatment at approximately 580°C applied to as-cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic HEA will induce coherent L12 nano-precipitates in the fcc lamellae, increasing yield strength by ~30% with only a minor (<3%) reduction in ductility.
candidates.intervention: Single isothermal aging treatment at ~580°C for an optimized time (e.g., on the order of minutes to an hour) to precipitate coherent ordered L12 particles in the fcc phase.

candidates.hypothesis: A single-step hybrid thermo-mechanical processing intervention consisting of cryo‑rolling (to induce high defect density) followed immediately by warm‑rolling at ~600°C on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA will create dual structural heterogeneities that elevate yield strength to ~2000 MPa while maintaining ductility around 8–10%.
candidates.intervention: Apply cryo‑rolling with a high strain (ε ~1.2) followed by warm‑rolling at 600°C with an equivalent strain increment, resulting in a total large reduction (around 90% thickness reduction).

candidates.hypothesis: A controlled, low‑temperature annealing step designed for phase‑selective recrystallization in a deformed eutectic HEA (e.g., Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2) will recrystallize the soft fcc phase while preserving the hard B2 phase skeleton, resulting in a ductility increase to ~35% uniform elongation with a true stress near 2 GPa.
candidates.intervention: Apply a tailored low‑temperature annealing treatment at a temperature sufficiently high to recrystallize the fcc phase but low enough to prevent full recrystallization of the B2 phase.

candidates.hypothesis: A low‑temperature annealing treatment below the recrystallization threshold, applied to as‐cast eutectic HEAs, will induce short‑range ordering (SRO) that forms nanoscale pseudo‐composite regions within the fcc phase, resulting in an increase of yield strength by ~10–20% with maintained or slightly improved ductility.
candidates.intervention: Perform a controlled low‑temperature anneal (e.g., at 300–400°C) for a duration that facilitates atomic diffusion on a few‐nanometer scale but avoids full recrystallization.

candidates.hypothesis: A controlled, low‑temperature annealing step designed for phase‑selective recrystallization in a deformed eutectic HEA (e.g., Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2) will recrystallize the soft fcc phase while preserving the hard B2 phase skeleton, resulting in a ductility increase to ~35% uniform elongation with a true stress near 2 GPa.
candidates.intervention: Apply a tailored low‑temperature annealing treatment at a temperature sufficiently high to recrystallize the fcc phase but low enough to prevent full recrystallization of the B2 phase.

candidates.hypothesis: A controlled low‐temperature annealing treatment at 300°C for 5 hours, applied in an inert atmosphere to as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA, will induce nanoscale short‐range ordering within the fcc lamellae, forming a pseudo‐composite microstructure that increases yield strength by approximately 15% (from ~770 MPa to ~885 MPa) while maintaining or slightly improving ductility (increasing elongation from ~18% to ~20%).
candidates.intervention: Perform a controlled anneal at 300°C for 5 hours under an inert atmosphere, ensuring atomic diffusion sufficient for SRO but below the recrystallization threshold.
candidates.changes: Clarified the annealing temperature and duration to a specific value (300°C for 5 hours) to promote short‐range ordering (SRO) without triggering full recrystallization or unwanted phase transformations; provided a quantitative ductility expectation and discussed mitigation of phase-change risks.

candidates.hypothesis: A tailored low‑temperature annealing treatment applied to a severely deformed Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 eutectic HEA will selectively recrystallize the soft fcc phase while preserving the skeletal hard B2 phase, resulting in a microstructure with fully recrystallized, equiaxed fcc grains that boosts uniform elongation to approximately 35% and elevates true stress to near 2 GPa.
candidates.intervention: Apply a precisely controlled, low‑temperature annealing process that is just above the recrystallization threshold for the fcc phase but below that for the B2 phase, following severe deformation.
candidates.changes: Emphasized the precision required in low-temperature annealing to achieve phase-selective recrystallization; clarified that the method applies to Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 and detailed the microstructural targets and necessary control of temperature and time.

candidates.hypothesis: A combined single intervention where Al0.7CoCrFeNi eutectic HEA is first lightly cold-deformed (by ~3% strain) and then subjected to a short isothermal aging treatment at 580°C for an optimized duration will induce the formation of coherent, uniformly dispersed L12 nano-precipitates in the fcc lamellae while maintaining precipitate‐free channels, yielding an increase in yield strength by ~30% (from ~770 MPa to ~1000–1080 MPa) with virtually unchanged or slightly improved ductility (approximately 17–18% elongation).
candidates.intervention: Apply a modest cold deformation (~3% strain) immediately followed by an isothermal aging treatment at 580°C for a controlled time (e.g., 10–30 minutes) under inert conditions.
candidates.changes: Addressed reviewers’ concerns by incorporating a slight pre-deformation step (to generate beneficial precipitate‐free channels) before aging to enhance ductility retention, and clarified processing parameters for isothermal aging at 580°C. This modification ensures that the improvement in strength does not come at the cost of ductility.

candidates.hypothesis: A single, integrated hybrid thermo-mechanical processing route—comprising cryo‑rolling (with a strain increment of ~1.2) immediately followed by warm‑rolling at 600°C (with an equivalent strain increment), conducted under controlled inert conditions—will transform cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA into a dual heterogeneous microstructure that raises yield strength to approximately 2000 MPa while maintaining ductility at around 8–10% elongation.
candidates.intervention: Apply an integrated processing route where the alloy is first cryo-rolled (imparting a strain of ~1.2) and then immediately warm-rolled at 600°C (imparting an additional strain of ~1.2), targeting an overall high strain (≈90% thickness reduction), with both stages performed in inert atmospheres.
